problem_motivation.content: Understanding perfusion in soft porous materials is needed because it is essential in biological and laboratory systems.
problem_motivation.evidence_span: Perfusion of soft materials such as biological tissue or hydrogels is essential for the functioning of organ and laboratory systems such as chromatographic columns and bioreactors.

problem_motivation.content: Coupling between wall mechanics and compaction from deformable confining boundaries has not yet been explored.

problem_motivation.content: How boundary compliance augments compaction-limited flow remains unresolved.
problem_motivation.evidence_span: Understanding how the compaction-limited ﬂow is augmented by the boundary compliance is important for interpreting transport in soft media but remains an open question

problem_motivation.content: Numerical steady solutions alone do not reveal how wall compliance alters the compacted rigid-wall state.
problem_motivation.evidence_span: The numerical solution of (II.38) determines the full steady response, but does not im-mediately reveal how wall compliance modiﬁes the compacted, rigid-wall state

problem_motivation.content: Several extensions are needed to broaden the range of systems the model can describe.

prior_approach.content: Parker et al. theoretically and experimentally analyzed compaction in porous media with rigid boundaries.
prior_approach.evidence_span: Generic models of compaction in porous media conﬁned by rigid boundaries were analysed theoretically and experimentally by Parker, et al. [3]

prior_approach.content: Hewitt et al. more recently analyzed rigid-boundary compaction models.
prior_approach.evidence_span: and more recently by Hewitt, et al. [4]

prior_approach.content: Strongly coupled poroelastic regimes are often modeled with fully nonlinear elasticity and solved numerically.
prior_approach.evidence_span: Poroelastic regimes with strong ﬂow–structure coupling are often treated with fully non-linear elastic models, for which numerical solutions are typically the only practical route

prior_approach.content: MacMinn et al. proposed a hybrid model with nonlinear kinematics but small-strain linear elasticity.
prior_approach.evidence_span: MacMinn et al. [23] suggested a hybrid approach that retains nonlinear kinematic links between strain, porosity, and permeability but models the solid’s constitutive law as small-strain linearly elastic

prior_approach.content: Hewitt et al. adopted the hybrid approach with Kozeny-Carman permeability and porosity-dependent stiffness.
prior_approach.evidence_span: This hybrid ap-proach was adopted with success by Hewitt et al. [4], who coupled a deformation-dependent Kozeny–Carman law to an eﬀective matrix stiﬀness scaling inversely with liquid volume fraction

prior_approach.content: Fiori et al. used Hewitt-like models for periodic loading and later extended them to solute transport.
prior_approach.evidence_span: Fiori et al. [24] used models similar to Hewitt’s to understand the eﬀect of periodic loading, and later extended the framework to include solute transport [25]

prior_approach.content: Bouckley et al. studied variants including gravity and external forcing.
prior_approach.evidence_span: Variations of Hewitt’s problem were explored by Bouckley et al. [26], including ﬂow against gravity and external mechanical forcing

prior_approach.content: Bouckley et al. generalized effective-stiffness laws using negative volume-fraction exponents.
prior_approach.evidence_span: [26] generalized eﬀective-stiﬀness laws proportional to volume frac-tion raised to a negative exponent

prior_approach.content: Related 1D compaction models couple porosity-dependent permeability with viscoelastic or viscoplastic response under fast loading.
prior_approach.evidence_span: Related one-dimensional compaction models for soft, satu-rated media [27, 28] couple porosity-dependent permeability to viscoelastic or viscoplastic solid response under fast time-dependent loading

prior_approach.content: The Mackenzie effective-modulus model was derived by upscaling linear elasticity around spherical pores.
prior_approach.evidence_span: These will be the Mackenzie model of eﬀective bulk and shear moduli given in full in Appendix F and derived in [33], which are found by upscaling the equations of linear elasticity around spherical pores

prior_approach.content: One-dimensional model and experiments of Hewitt et al. previously reported the plateau behavior
prior_approach.evidence_span: producing a plateau consistent with the one-dimensional model and experiments of [4].

prior_approach.content: Rigid-wall experimental comparison uses Hewitt's large-S compaction theory as the appropriate model
prior_approach.evidence_span: The blue solid curve corresponds to experiments with a rigid outer wall, for which the deformation is essentially one-dimensional and the appropriate model is the large-S limit of Hewitt’s compaction theory.

prior_approach.content: This study extends Hewitt et al.'s one-dimensional compaction model to a cylindrical porous medium with a deformable membrane.
prior_approach.evidence_span: In this study we extended the one-dimensional compaction model of Hewitt et al. [4] to a tall, thin cylindrical porous medium with a laterally deformable, impermeable elastic membrane.

prior_approach.content: Bouckley et al. studied one-dimensional soft media classification by flux response to pressure drop aligned with gravity.
prior_approach.evidence_span: A natural point of comparison is the recent one-dimensional study of Bouckley et al. [26], who classify soft media by how the flux responds to a pressure drop applied in the direction of gravity.

prior_approach.content: In Bouckley et al.'s framework, large-pressure behavior is set by permeability and effective-stiffness exponents, with type-1 showing ever-increasing flux and type-2 showing a finite plateau.
prior_approach.evidence_span: In their framework, with pressure-driven flow aligned with gravity and both ends mechanically constrained, the large-pressure behaviour is controlled entirely by the exponents in the permeability and effective-stiffness laws: “type-1” media have an ever-increasing flux, whereas “type-2” media develop a finite compaction plateau whose existence and height depend on the balance of these exponents.

prior_limitation.content: The full analytical membrane solution is numerically inconvenient because the equation is singular for small T.

rejected_alternative.content: Rather than prior 1D/rigid-boundary treatments, this study extends the same hybrid philosophy to a 2D radially compliant cylindrical geometry.
rejected_alternative.evidence_span: In this study, we follow the same hybrid linear/nonlinear philosophy, but extend it to a two-dimensional, radially compliant cylindrical geometry

rejected_alternative.content: To isolate wall compliance, the study uses clamped ends instead of more compliant end conditions.
rejected_alternative.evidence_span: To fully isolate the role of wall compliance, we impose clamped boundary conditions

rejected_alternative.content: Instead of the full coupled system, the rest of the study uses the simplified uncoupled system because the simplification is justified.
rejected_alternative.evidence_span: for the rest of the study we focus on the simpliﬁed system (II.32) and (II.24)

rejected_alternative.content: Rather than using the full analytical solution directly, the authors solve the membrane equation by matched asymptotics because of numerical difficulty from singularity.
rejected_alternative.evidence_span: We therefore solve (II.32) according to (II.26) via matched asymptotics

rejected_alternative.content: The paper rejects the idea that plateau formation is controlled only by poroelastic exponents, showing radial compliance changes that conclusion.
rejected_alternative.evidence_span: Our work complements Bouckley et al. by showing that once radial compliance is admitted, the presence or absence of a plateau is no longer determined solely by the poroelastic exponents.

rejected_alternative.content: Unlike strictly one-dimensional fixed-boundary columns, the present two-dimensional setting permits reorganized regimes and super-Darcy flow.
rejected_alternative.evidence_span: their exploration of how varying the permeability and stiffness exponents moves a one-dimensional system between plateau-forming and non-plateau-forming classes is extended here into a two-dimensional setting where an additional degree of freedom reorganizes those regimes and allows for behaviours such as super-Darcy flow that cannot arise in a strictly one-dimensional column with fixed boundaries.

inspiration_source.content: The study is motivated by applications in organs, chromatographic columns, and bioreactors.
inspiration_source.evidence_span: Inspired by these applications, we model ﬂuid-driven compaction in a long, thin cylindrical porous medium bounded by an impermeable elastic membrane and study how ﬂow regimes relate to elastic parameters.

inspiration_source.content: The Mackenzie model is adopted because it is widely applicable at small porosity and extends the modulus used by Hewitt et al.
inspiration_source.evidence_span: it is considered a widely applicable model for media with small porosity [5], and is a direct two-dimensional extension of the eﬀective modulus used in [4]

inspiration_source.content: The rigid-wall limit is framed by analogy to Bouckley et al.'s type-2 class.
inspiration_source.evidence_span: For the constitutive choices adopted here, the rigid-wall limit of our model behaves in an analogous way to their type-2 class.

causal_claim.content: Compliant walls allow flow to increase beyond an intermediate plateau once imposed pressure reaches a threshold set by membrane stiffness and initial porosity.
causal_claim.evidence_span: Whereas rigid boundaries produce a compaction plateau, compliant walls exhibit, at most, an intermediate plateau beyond which the ﬂow increases once the imposed pressure becomes comparable to the product of membrane stiﬀness and initial porosity.

causal_claim.content: A membrane softer than the porous medium can cause flow rates to exceed those of a rigid medium.
causal_claim.evidence_span: When the membrane is less stiﬀthan the porous medium, ﬂow rate can exceed that expected for a rigid medium.

causal_claim.content: Pressure gradients compact porous media, shrinking pores and feeding back on flow.
causal_claim.evidence_span: compact under forced perfusion due to ﬂuid pressure gradients that shrink pore space and feed back to the ﬂow

causal_claim.content: Matrix compression reduces permeability.
causal_claim.evidence_span: This coupling reduces the permeability of a porous medium as its matrix compresses

causal_claim.content: Beyond a threshold, increasing driving pressure no longer increases throughput because of a compaction plateau.
causal_claim.evidence_span: beyond a certain point, additional driving pressure yields no extra throughput due to a compaction ﬂow-rate plateau

causal_claim.content: Pressure gradients that drive perfusion can also compact tissue, reduce permeability, and affect transport.
causal_claim.evidence_span: the same pressure gradients that drive ﬂow can compact the tissue, reduce permeability and impact transport

causal_claim.content: Elevated interstitial pressure and matrix remodeling can restrict perfusion in tumors.
causal_claim.evidence_span: elevated interstitial pressure and matrix remodeling can restrict perfusion [11]

causal_claim.content: Boundary compliance can relieve a compaction-induced flow plateau.
causal_claim.evidence_span: understanding when compaction can produce a plateau in ﬂow and when boundary compliance can relieve that plateau is important

causal_claim.content: Semi-rigid confinement changes pathway formation and breakthrough behavior compared with rigid confinement.
causal_claim.evidence_span: gas migration through bentonite under semi-rigid (transversely compliant) conﬁnement exhibits diﬀerent pathway formation and breakthrough behaviour than under rigid conﬁnement

causal_claim.content: Different stiffness-law exponents select different qualitative flow-rate regimes.
causal_claim.evidence_span: which identify how diﬀerent exponents select diﬀerent qualitative ﬂow-rate regimes

causal_claim.content: If the membrane is much stiffer than the porous medium and pressure, the model recovers Hewitt's 1D plateauing behavior.
causal_claim.evidence_span: When the membrane is much stiﬀer than the porous medium and the pressure driving the ﬂow, the model we develop recovers the one-dimensional plateauing model of Hewitt et al. [4]

causal_claim.content: Once driving pressure exceeds membrane stiffness times initial porosity, flow departs from the plateau.
causal_claim.evidence_span: but diverges from the plateau when the driving pressure rises above the product of membrane stiﬀness and initial porosity

causal_claim.content: Moderately large membrane-to-medium stiffness ratios produce diverging flow without an intermediate plateau.
causal_claim.evidence_span: When the stiﬀness ratio of membrane to porous medium is only moderately large, we observe a diverging ﬂow rate with no intermediate plateau

causal_claim.content: Small membrane-to-medium stiffness ratios yield flow rates above the rigid-medium expectation.
causal_claim.evidence_span: When the ratio is small, we observe a ﬂow rate larger than would be expected for a rigid medium

causal_claim.content: Neglecting porosity-dependent terms in the membrane equation reduces computational cost by uncoupling the system.
causal_claim.evidence_span: the solution for χ(z) substituted into (II.24) uncoupling the system and reducing unnecessary computational cost

causal_claim.content: Wall compliance causes departure from the rigid-wall compaction plateau.
causal_claim.evidence_span: identiﬁes how wall compliance produces departure from the rigid-wall compaction plateau

causal_claim.content: More compliant boundary causes radial expansion, reducing local axial compression
causal_claim.evidence_span: Figure 2(b) shows the same pressure load (P = 8.9 × 102, L = 0) but with a more compliant boundary (S = 104), so that the membrane expands outwards radially. In this regime the cylinder expands radially in the middle of its length, reducing the axial compression locally.

causal_claim.content: Reduced axial compression keeps porosity near inlet value over more of the column and lowers vertical Darcy velocity in the bulged region
causal_claim.evidence_span: As a result the porosity remains close to its inlet value over a much larger fraction of the column, and the vertical Darcy velocity is reduced in the bulging region where the cross-section is largest.

causal_claim.content: Higher hydrostatic pressure at the bottom causes stronger outward bowing there
causal_claim.evidence_span: The lower part of the column carries most of the compaction, and the membrane bows outward more strongly toward the bottom where the hydrostatic pressure is highest.

causal_claim.content: Asymmetric bowing generates vertical asymmetry in porosity and Darcy velocity
causal_claim.evidence_span: This generates a corresponding vertical asymmetry in porosity and Darcy velocity.

causal_claim.content: Decreasing bending parameter weakens bending resistance and makes radial expansion profile flatter and more plug-like
causal_claim.evidence_span: Decreasing T weakens bending resistance and produces a ﬂatter, more plug-like radial expansion in the interior, with the membrane curvature conﬁned to narrow boundary layers near the clamped ends.

causal_claim.content: Small pressure gives Darcy-like linear flow because the matrix is essentially uncompressed
causal_claim.evidence_span: For small P, all curves follow the Darcy prediction for a rigid medium: the porous matrix is essentially uncompressed, and the ﬂow rate is proportional to pressure.

causal_claim.content: Increasing pressure causes outlet-near axial compaction and a flow-rate plateau
causal_claim.evidence_span: As P increases, the porous matrix compacts axially near the outlet and the ﬂow rate ceases to grow, producing a plateau consistent with the one-dimensional model and experiments of [4].

causal_claim.content: When pressure exceeds membrane stiffness times initial porosity, flow departs from the plateau and rises again
causal_claim.evidence_span: As predicted by the asymptotic analysis in section II C, divergence from the plateau values occurs once P becomes larger than the product of membrane stiﬀness S and initial porosity Φ, allowing the ﬂow rate to increase again.

causal_claim.content: Increasing pressure causes central membrane bulging
causal_claim.evidence_span: As P increases, the membrane bulges outward over the central portion of the cylinder

causal_claim.content: When pressure becomes comparable to Φ(S+2), membrane bulging causes deviation from Darcy prediction
causal_claim.evidence_span: As P becomes comparable to Φ(S + 2) the membrane bulges and deviates from the Darcy prediction.

causal_claim.content: Softening the wall lets radial dilation offset compaction and can raise flow above the rigid-medium value
causal_claim.evidence_span: As the wall is softened, radial dilation of the column increasingly oﬀsets this compaction, and for the softest admissible wall in panel (a), S = 0.2, the average porosity rises enough that Q0 exceeds the rigid-medium value, giving a weakly super-Darcy response.

causal_claim.content: Gravity-driven curves leave Darcy scaling once L becomes order 1
causal_claim.evidence_span: The curves again depart from Darcy scaling once L becomes O(1), but gravity is eﬀectively weaker than the imposed pressure.

causal_claim.content: For S>1, increasing pressure drives axial compaction and makes flow sub-Darcy
causal_claim.evidence_span: Immediately above this band for S > 1 lies the green sub-Darcy region, where increasing P drives axial compaction and the ﬂow rate lags behind the rigid-medium prediction.

causal_claim.content: At very large stiffness, sub-Darcy behavior feeds into a compaction plateau where changing P or S barely changes flow
causal_claim.evidence_span: At very large stiﬀness, S ≳103, this feeds into a triangular orange region in which a compaction plateau forms. Changing P or S within this region does not signiﬁcantly change Q0, as the system has reached the compacted state.

causal_claim.content: For any finite wall stiffness, sufficiently large pressure unblocks the system and flow diverges again
causal_claim.evidence_span: However, for all ﬁnite S, a value of P can be reached which unblocks the system and the ﬂow rate starts diverging again.

causal_claim.content: Crossing the dot-dashed curve means porosity rises above its initial value somewhere, separating global compaction from local dilation
causal_claim.evidence_span: The dot–dashed black curve indicates where the porosity starts to rise above the initial value, and hence separates globally compacted states (φ0(z) ≤Φ everywhere, on the south–east side of the curve) from solutions in which dilation occurs somewhere in the column (φ0(z) > Φ locally, to the north–west).

causal_claim.content: Changing porosity has little effect on map structure but strongly affects strain magnitude in proportion to Φ
causal_claim.evidence_span: Changing Φ has minimal impact on the overall structure of the parameter map, but strongly changes strain size which is proportional to Φ.

causal_claim.content: Changing bending parameter mainly shifts the φ0≤Φ boundary, with smaller T shrinking the valid granular-media region
causal_claim.evidence_span: Changing T also has little eﬀect on the map structure, apart from changing the location of φ0 ≤Φ curve (a smaller T leads to a smaller valid region for granular media).

causal_claim.content: Increasing pressure compacts the outlet region and drives the flow rate toward a compaction plateau.
causal_claim.evidence_span: Increasing pressure compacts the outlet region into a boundary layer and the flow rate approaches a genuine compaction plateau, beyond which additional forcing yields essentially no extra throughput.

causal_claim.content: Finite membrane stiffness qualitatively changes the flow-response behavior.
causal_claim.evidence_span: Allowing the membrane to be finitely stiff qualitatively reorganises this picture.

causal_claim.content: Outlet jamming and porosity collapse make the flow rate nearly pressure-independent.
causal_claim.evidence_span: The outlet region jams, the porosity collapses, and the flow rate becomes nearly pressure-independent.

causal_claim.content: When imposed pressure reaches the scale of membrane stiffness times initial porosity, wall inflation relieves outlet compaction and flow rises again.
causal_claim.evidence_span: Once the imposed pressure becomes comparable to the product of membrane stiffness and initial porosity the compliant wall inflates, relieving outlet compaction and allowing the flow rate to increase again.

causal_claim.content: Any finite wall compliance causes the flow-pressure curve to diverge eventually instead of saturating.
causal_claim.evidence_span: Thus, for any finite S the flow–pressure curve ultimately diverges rather than saturating.

causal_claim.content: Reducing stiffness makes radial expansion important at lower loads.
causal_claim.evidence_span: As S is reduced, radial expansion becomes important at progressively lower loads.

causal_claim.content: Lower stiffness shrinks and then removes the intermediate plateau, yielding only divergent responses.
causal_claim.evidence_span: The intermediate plateau shrinks and eventually disappears, leaving purely divergent responses

causal_claim.content: Responses are sub-Darcy when axial compaction dominates and super-Darcy when wall-driven dilation raises average porosity above its undeformed value.
causal_claim.evidence_span: leaving purely divergent responses that are sub-Darcy when axial compaction dominates and super-Darcy when wall-driven dilation allows the average porosity to rise above its undeformed value.

causal_claim.content: Any finite wall compliance destroys the terminal plateau and causes renewed divergence of flow rate.
causal_claim.evidence_span: Any finite wall compliance ultimately destroys the terminal plateau and leads to renewed divergence of the flow rate

causal_claim.content: Wall-stiffness ratio S becomes the key control parameter when radial compliance is included.
causal_claim.evidence_span: with the wall-stiffness ratio S taking over as the key control parameter.

causal_claim.content: When wall friction is negligible, the main fields, flow-pressure curves, and breakthrough criterion are unchanged except for higher-order effects.
causal_claim.evidence_span: in that regime φ0(z) and χ(z), the Q0–P/S curves, and the breakthrough criterion P/(S+2) = O(Φ) are unchanged up to higher–order corrections, with at most a mild thickening of axial boundary layers near z = 0, 1.

causal_claim.content: Only strong interfacial coupling or short/thick samples make wall friction reduce flow and shift onset.
causal_claim.evidence_span: Only for very strong interfacial coupling or short/thick samples such that ǫ Λ ≳1 does wall friction measurably reduce Q0 at fixed P/S and shift the onset.

causal_claim.content: Lowering undeformed porosity leaves the regime-map structure nearly unchanged but moves strain contours upward so the same behaviors occur at small strain.
causal_claim.evidence_span: Appendix K, Fig. 10 reproduces the main regime diagram with Φ reduced from 0.05 to 0.01 and shows that the qualitative structure of the map is essentially unchanged, while the strain contours shift upward so that the entire sequence of behaviours discussed in the paper (plateau, its breakthrough, its disappearance with wall compliance, and the transitions between sub-Darcy and super-Darcy regimes) occurs within an indisputably small-strain range, max |εzz| ≲0.02.

causal_claim.content: The observed phenomena are not artifacts of large-strain linear elasticity because they persist at very small strain.
causal_claim.evidence_span: This demonstrates that the phenomena we analyze are not artifacts of using linear elasticity at large strains; rather, they persist at very small strain and are therefore physically meaningful.

causal_claim.content: Transverse compliance qualitatively switches the flow-pressure relation rather than slightly perturbing one-dimensional compaction.
causal_claim.evidence_span: Taken together, our results highlight that transverse compliance is not a small perturbation to classic one-dimensional compaction, but a qualitative switch that reorganises the flow–pressure relation.

causal_claim.content: In the rigid-wall limit, the plateau is terminal, but any finite wall stiffness removes that terminal plateau.
causal_claim.evidence_span: In the strict rigid-wall limit the Hewitt–type plateau is genuinely terminal, but any finite wall stiffness ultimately destroys this terminal plateau.

causal_claim.content: When driving pressure reaches the scale of membrane stiffness times initial porosity, radial expansion relieves outlet compaction and flow diverges again.
causal_claim.evidence_span: Once the driving pressure becomes comparable to the product of membrane stiffness and initial porosity, radial expansion relieves outlet compaction and the flow rate diverges again.

causal_claim.content: Large S gives a long intermediate plateau like the rigid case, whereas moderate and small S suppress the plateau and produce divergent sub- or super-Darcy responses.
causal_claim.evidence_span: Large S yields an extended intermediate plateau that mimics the rigid case over several decades in pressure, whereas moderate and small S suppress this plateau and produce purely divergent responses that can be either sub-Darcy or super-Darcy depending on the balance between axial compaction and wall-driven dilation.

causal_claim.content: When P + L exceeds 1, a boundary layer forms and this slows convergence.
causal_claim.evidence_span: With P + L > 1, the boundary layer forms, slowing convergence.

causal_claim.content: Reducing undeformed porosity shifts strain contours upward and enlarges the low-strain validity region.
causal_claim.evidence_span: the family of strain contours (shown in white) shifts upward in the (P, S) plane, enlarging the low–strain validity wedge

causal_claim.content: Undeformed porosity acts as a control parameter for overall strain level.
causal_claim.evidence_span: Thus Φ acts as a convenient control parameter for the overall strain level.

causal_claim.content: Further decreasing undeformed porosity moves the same behaviors to even smaller strains.
causal_claim.evidence_span: Decreasing Φ further pushes these behaviours to even smaller strains.

causal_claim.content: Smaller initial porosity enables the described behaviors to be captured at smaller strains.
causal_claim.evidence_span: This shows that smaller initial porosity allows the described behaviours to be captured at even smaller strains.

causal_claim.content: Lowering T leaves the diagram nearly unchanged except for shifting the φ0(z) ≤ Φ contour southeast, which reduces the region that can plausibly represent disconnected media.
causal_claim.evidence_span: Again, the diagram remains almost unchanged, except that the φ0(z) ≤ Φ contour is shifted southeast, reducing the portion of the map that can credibly model disconnected media.

hypothesis_statement.content: The study proposes that relative wall compliance reorganizes the flow-pressure relation in a compliant cylindrical porous medium.

hypothesis_statement.content: The authors choose porosity-dependent permeability and elastic moduli intended to be broadly applicable.
hypothesis_statement.evidence_span: our choices for the porosity-dependent permeability k∗(φ) and eﬀective bulk and shear moduli of the porous medium K∗(φ) and G∗(φ), which we choose to be the most widely applicable

hypothesis_statement.content: The study selects constitutive laws judged to be the most widely representative.

hypothesis_statement.content: Wall friction is negligible when the aspect-ratio-scaled interfacial shear parameter is small.

evidence_result.content: An asymptotic solution for negligible gravity captures departure from the plateau and provides compact formulas for effective permeability and flow rate.
